stimuli.title: The lunch-box relay
stimuli.content:
Every working day in some large Indian cities, thousands of home-cooked lunches travel from kitchens in the suburbs to offices in the business district, and the empty boxes return home the same evening. The service is run not by a technology company but by a network of carriers, most of whom have little formal schooling. Yet the boxes almost never go missing.

The secret lies in a simple system. Each box is marked with a short code of letters, numbers and colours painted on its lid. The code shows the station where the box is collected, the station where it is to be delivered, and the building and floor of the office. Carriers do not need to read addresses; they need only to recognise the marks. At every major station, boxes are sorted by code and handed from one team to the next, much like a baton in a relay race.

Timing is just as important as sorting. The carriers depend on local trains, which run to a fixed timetable, and each team knows exactly which train it must catch. A delay of even a few minutes at one point can upset the whole chain, so carriers take great pride in being punctual. Many of them work in the same area for years and come to know their customers by sight.

The system has drawn visitors from business schools and large companies, who come to study how such reliability is achieved without computers. What they often find is that the strength of the network lies less in its tools than in its people: a shared sense of duty, clear roles and a habit of helping a team-mate who falls behind.

The service has had to adapt in recent years. Some customers now book through mobile apps, and food-delivery companies offer competition. Even so, many families still prefer to send food from their own kitchens, and the painted code on the lid continues to do its quiet work.

stimuli.title: The sleepy classroom
stimuli.content:
Teachers of early-morning classes know the scene well: rows of students yawning, heads resting on hands, eyes struggling to stay open. It is tempting to blame late-night phone use, and screens certainly play a part. But sleep scientists point to a deeper cause. During the teenage years, the body clock shifts, so that adolescents naturally begin to feel sleepy later at night than younger children or adults do. A fifteen-year-old who is sent to bed at nine may simply lie awake.

This shift would matter little if teenagers could also wake later. Instead, many schools begin their day early, and long journeys mean that some students leave home before sunrise. The result is a steady loss of sleep through the week, which students try to recover by sleeping late on Saturdays and Sundays. Researchers call this pattern 'social jet lag', because the body is pushed back and forth as if it were crossing time zones every weekend.

The costs go beyond yawning. Students who sleep too little find it harder to concentrate and to remember what they have learnt, and they are more likely to feel irritable or low. Tired teenagers are also more prone to accidents, especially on two-wheelers.

A few schools in different countries have experimented with starting classes later in the morning, often by thirty to sixty minutes. Studies of such schools have generally found that students sleep longer, attend more regularly and arrive less tired, though the effect on examination results varies. The change is not easy to make: bus routes must be rearranged, parents' working hours must be considered, and sports and other activities may be pushed into the evening.

Sleep experts do not claim that a later bell will solve every problem. Their point is narrower but important. A sleepy teenager is not necessarily lazy; he or she may be fighting biology. Schools that take this into account may find that the same lessons, taught an hour later, are better received.

stimuli.title: The magic of ninety-nine
stimuli.content:
Walk into almost any shop and you will see prices such as ₹199, ₹499 or ₹9,999. Few sellers choose these numbers by accident. A price that ends just below a round figure is known as a 'charm price', and retailers have used it for more than a century in the belief that it makes goods seem cheaper than they are.

The belief is not entirely mistaken. Researchers who have studied shoppers' behaviour suggest that people tend to read a price from left to right and give most weight to the first digit. A price of ₹499 is therefore registered as 'four hundred and something' rather than as almost five hundred. The saving of a single rupee is trivial, but the impression of a lower price category can be strong, especially when a shopper is in a hurry or comparing many items at once.

Charm prices also carry a message. Shoppers have learnt to associate them with discounts and bargains, so a price ending in 99 can signal value even when no discount is being offered. For the same reason, sellers of luxury goods often avoid them. A jeweller or a high-end restaurant is more likely to quote a round ₹5,000, which suggests quality and confidence rather than a hunt for bargains.

The effect has limits. When buyers think carefully, as they do before purchasing a house or a car, the pull of the first digit weakens. Some studies have found little or no effect for certain products, and the results vary from one market to another. In addition, as digital payments replace cash, the practical nuisance of receiving small change has disappeared, which may alter how shoppers respond to odd prices.

Still, the persistence of the ninety-nine suggests that sellers find it useful. It is a reminder that a price is not just a number but a piece of communication, and that buyers, however rational they believe themselves to be, read more into it than arithmetic alone would justify.

stimuli.title: A garden plant gone wild
stimuli.content:
In the nineteenth century, a flowering shrub from Central and South America was brought to India as an ornamental plant for gardens. Its small, bright flowers made it popular, and it was later planted along fences and railway lines as a hedge. Today that shrub, lantana, covers vast areas of Indian forests, and ecologists count it among the most troublesome invasive plants in the country.

Lantana spreads with remarkable ease. Birds eat its berries and scatter the seeds widely, and the plant grows quickly in open, disturbed ground, such as the edges of roads or patches cleared by fire. Once established, it forms dense thickets that shade out the grasses and young trees beneath. Because most animals avoid eating its leaves, which are toxic to livestock, there is little to keep it in check.

The consequences reach well beyond the plants it smothers. Grazing animals such as deer find less to eat where lantana dominates, and the predators that depend on them may follow them elsewhere. Villagers who once collected fodder, fuel and medicinal herbs from the forest floor find these resources harder to reach. The thickets can also feed forest fires, since the dry stems burn readily.

Removing lantana has proved difficult. Cutting it back without digging out the roots often leads to vigorous regrowth, and cleared ground is quickly reinvaded unless native grasses are planted at once. Some forest departments have therefore adopted a method in which each plant is uprooted at the base and the area is restored with local species, but the work is slow and labour-intensive.

A few communities have found an unexpected use for the plant. Its tough, flexible stems can be woven into furniture and baskets, and craftspeople trained in this work earn an income while helping to clear the forest. Such efforts cannot remove lantana on their own, given the scale of the problem, but they turn a burden into a modest resource and give local people a reason to keep up the fight.

stimuli.title: Money already spent
stimuli.content:
Suppose you have paid in advance for a concert ticket, and on the evening of the show you feel unwell and the rain is pouring down. Many people would go anyway, reasoning that they cannot let the money go to waste. Yet the money is gone whether they go or not. The only question that remains is whether the evening will be better spent at the concert or at home. Economists call money that has already been spent and cannot be recovered a 'sunk cost', and they argue that it should play no part in decisions about the future.

The advice is simple to state and remarkably hard to follow. People dislike admitting that an earlier choice was a mistake, and abandoning a project can feel like confirming that the resources put into it were wasted. So they continue, sometimes adding more money in the hope of rescuing what has already been spent. Psychologists have found this tendency in individuals, in companies and in governments, and it tends to grow stronger when the person who made the original decision is also the one deciding whether to continue.

Large organisations offer the most expensive examples. A half-built project may consume further funds for years because stopping it would mean writing off the amount already invested and accepting blame for the original plan. Officials may describe the extra spending as 'protecting the investment', a phrase that quietly shifts attention from future returns to past costs.

Not every decision to persist is irrational, however. Sometimes the money already spent has bought something of real value, such as a nearly finished building, a skilled team or knowledge gained through trial and error, that makes completing the project cheaper than starting something new. In such cases, continuing is justified not by the past spending itself but by what it has produced. The difficulty lies in telling the two situations apart honestly.

Some institutions try to do this by separating roles: the people who review a troubled project are not the ones who proposed it. Others set conditions in advance, agreeing at the outset on the point at which a venture will be abandoned. Neither method is foolproof, but both rest on the same insight: the past should inform our judgement of the future, not hold it hostage.

stimuli.title: The pull of the crowd
stimuli.content:
A telephone is useless to the first person who owns one; its value comes entirely from the number of other people one can call. Economists call this a 'network effect': a product or service becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it. Messaging apps, online marketplaces and even languages share this property, and it shapes competition in ways that ordinary products do not.

When network effects are strong, early leads tend to grow. A marketplace with many sellers attracts more buyers, whose presence draws still more sellers. A rival with a better design may struggle to break in, because a customer who switches gives up access to everyone who stays behind. Markets of this kind often tip towards one or two dominant firms, not necessarily because those firms offer the best product but because they reached a large size first.

For users, the outcome is mixed. A single dominant network is convenient: everyone can reach everyone else, and there is no need to juggle several accounts. But a firm that knows its customers cannot easily leave has less reason to keep prices low or to listen to complaints. It may raise the fees it charges to sellers, change its rules without warning or neglect the privacy of its users, confident that few will walk away.

Regulators have experimented with several responses. One is to require 'interoperability', so that the users of one service can communicate or trade with the users of another, much as subscribers of different mobile operators can call one another. Another is to let users carry their data, such as contacts or ratings, when they move to a competitor, which lowers the cost of switching. A third is to build a shared platform on which many firms compete, so that the network itself belongs to no single company.

None of these remedies is free of difficulty. Interoperability can be technically complex and may weaken security if it is designed carelessly, and forcing a network open may reduce the reward for building one in the first place. The challenge is to keep the benefits of a large network, which are real, while preventing its owner from turning those benefits into a toll that users have no choice but to pay.

stimuli.title: Keepers of the light
stimuli.content:
For centuries, lighthouses have warned ships away from rocks and shallow water. Before modern navigation equipment, a sailor approaching the coast at night (1) ______ on these lights to know where he was. Each lighthouse flashes in its own pattern, so that an experienced crew can tell one from another.

Running a lighthouse was once a demanding job. Keepers lived at the station with their families, often on a lonely headland or a small island. They climbed the tower every evening to light the lamp, cleaned the glass so that the beam would not be (2) ______, and kept watch through the night. In stormy weather, they could not leave their post even for a short while.

Over the last few decades, most lighthouses have been (3) ______. Electric lamps now switch on by themselves at dusk, and faults are reported to a distant control room. Satellite navigation has also made the lights far less (4) ______ than they once were. As a result, the old job of the keeper has almost disappeared.

The towers themselves, however, have found new life. Several have been opened to visitors, who climb the narrow stairs to enjoy the view and learn about the history of the coast. Small museums explain how the great lenses work and how the keepers lived. For many coastal towns, the lighthouse has become a (5) ______ that draws tourists and their money.

Sailors still value the lights, too. Electronic systems can fail, and a captain who sees a familiar beam in the darkness knows at once whether his instruments are telling him the (6) ______.

stimuli.title: Mushrooms from straw
stimuli.content:
Every year, after the paddy harvest, farmers in parts of northern India are left with mountains of straw. With little time before the next crop must be sown, many set the fields on fire, sending thick smoke across the region. The practice is (1) ______ by law in many places, yet it continues because the alternatives seem costly or slow.

One alternative turns the problem into a (2) ______. Paddy straw, when chopped, soaked and packed into beds, makes an excellent base for growing certain varieties of mushroom. A small shed, some plastic sheeting and a few weeks of care are enough to produce a crop that can be sold in nearby towns. The leftover material, rich in organic matter, can then be (3) ______ to the fields as manure, improving the soil that produced the straw in the first place.

The idea is not new, but it has spread slowly. Mushrooms are delicate and spoil within days, so growers need quick access to buyers. Many farmers also lack the knowledge needed to keep the beds free of disease. Where cooperatives have stepped in to provide (4) ______ and to collect the produce, the results have been encouraging, and some women's groups now earn a steady income from their mushroom sheds.

Mushroom growing cannot, of course, use all the straw that a region produces. It is one of several (5) ______, along with machines that mix the straw into the soil and plants that turn it into fuel. Together, such measures can reduce burning, but only if farmers find them practical and (6) ______. A ban that offers no workable alternative is likely to be ignored, however strictly it is worded.

stimuli.title: Gold in the vault
stimuli.content:
Long after the world abandoned the gold standard, central banks continue to hold large stocks of gold. To some observers this seems **(1) reasonable**: gold pays no interest, costs money to store and guard, and its price can swing sharply from one year to the next. Why should a modern central bank keep so much of its reserves in a metal that earns nothing?

Part of the answer lies in trust. Unlike a government bond, gold is not anyone's promise to pay, so it cannot be **(2) defaulted** on, and if it is stored at home it cannot be frozen by a foreign government. In times of crisis, when confidence in currencies and financial institutions weakens, gold has tended to hold its value or even rise, which makes it a **(3) risky** hedge against turmoil.

Gold also helps central banks **(4) concentrate** their reserves. A reserve portfolio made up mainly of assets in a single foreign currency leaves a country exposed to that currency's ups and downs; adding gold spreads the risk. In recent years, several central banks in emerging economies have been **(5) reducing** their gold holdings steadily, partly for this reason and partly to lessen their dependence on any one country's financial system.

The case is not without critics. They point out that the price of gold is driven largely by sentiment, and that money tied up in the metal could instead earn interest in bonds. Holding some gold, they concede, may be prudent, but holding a great deal of it amounts to **(6) costly** insurance whose benefits are hard to measure.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what information does the code painted on each lunch box show?

options.text: The name of the cook and the time at which the food was made
The price of the meal and the telephone number of the customer
The collection station, the delivery station and the office location
The name of the carrier and the number of the train he must take

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the code 'shows the station where the box is collected, the station where it is to be delivered, and the building and floor of the office'.
steps: Three items: collection station, delivery station, building and floor
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and D list details the passage never says are in the code. D is tempting because trains are mentioned in paragraph 3, but the code describes the box's route, not the carrier or his train.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The collection station, the delivery station and the office location

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why does the author compare the handling of the boxes to 'a baton in a relay race'?

options.text: Boxes are passed from one team to the next at each major station.
Carriers often have to run hard to catch their trains on time.
Teams compete with one another to deliver their boxes first.
Each carrier takes his boxes the whole way from home to office.

solution.concept: Inference: what a comparison refers to
solution.explanation: The comparison comes right after the statement that boxes 'are sorted by code and handed from one team to the next'. In a relay race the baton is passed from one runner to the next; the boxes pass from team to team in the same way.
steps: Read the clause the comparison is attached to
Boxes are handed from one team to the next
A baton passes from runner to runner: option A
solution.why_others_wrong: B picks up the idea of running, but the comparison is attached to the handing over, not to catching trains. C invents a competition the passage never mentions. D contradicts the idea of passing the boxes on.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Boxes are passed from one team to the next at each major station.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What do visitors from business schools and companies often find when they study the network?

options.text: Its success rests mainly on modern computers and tracking tools.
Its strength lies more in its people and their habits than in tools.
Its carriers are paid far more than most office workers in the city.
It works only because local trains in the city are never late.

solution.concept: Locating a stated finding
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says visitors 'often find ... that the strength of the network lies less in its tools than in its people: a shared sense of duty, clear roles and a habit of helping a team-mate'.
steps: Find 'What they often find' in paragraph 4
Strength lies 'less in its tools than in its people'
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts 'without computers'. C is never mentioned. D goes too far: trains run to a timetable, but the passage says a delay can upset the chain, so it does not claim trains are never late.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Its strength lies more in its people and their habits than in tools.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'upset' as used in the passage ('A delay of even a few minutes at one point can upset the whole chain')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: upset (a plan or system) = disturb its normal working
solution.explanation: A delay at one point throws the rest of the timetable out of order. 'Upset' here means disturb or disrupt the smooth working of the chain.
steps: Subject: a delay; object: the whole chain (of hand-overs)
Effect: the chain stops working smoothly
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Sadden', 'annoy' and 'worry' are the emotional senses of 'upset', used of people's feelings. A chain of deliveries has no feelings; a delay throws it out of order.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to sleep scientists, what is the deeper cause of teenagers' sleepiness in early-morning classes?

options.text: Heavy meals eaten late in the evening just before going to bed
Classrooms that are too warm and poorly lit early in the morning
Homework that keeps most of them working until after midnight
A shift in the body clock that delays their sleepiness at night

solution.concept: Locating a stated cause
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'sleep scientists point to a deeper cause. During the teenage years, the body clock shifts, so that adolescents naturally begin to feel sleepy later at night'.
steps: Next sentence: the body clock shifts
solution.why_others_wrong: Meals (A), classrooms (B) and homework (C) are never mentioned. The only other cause named, phone use, is described as playing a part but not as the deeper cause.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A shift in the body clock that delays their sleepiness at night

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why do researchers call the pattern described in paragraph 2 'social jet lag'?

options.text: Students travel very long distances to reach their schools each day.
Shifting sleep between weekdays and weekends is like crossing time zones.
Teenagers stay up late talking to friends who live in other countries.
School timetables in many places are set by the clocks of other nations.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains the name: 'because the body is pushed back and forth as if it were crossing time zones every weekend' (short sleep on weekdays, long sleep on Sundays).
steps: Reason given: the body is pushed back and forth as if crossing time zones
solution.why_others_wrong: A picks up 'long journeys' but that is not the reason for the name. C and D are not mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Shifting sleep between weekdays and weekends is like crossing time zones.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'prone' as used in the passage ('Tired teenagers are also more prone to accidents')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: prone to = likely to suffer from
solution.explanation: The sentence lists another cost of too little sleep. 'More prone to accidents' means more likely to have accidents.
steps: Context: costs of lack of sleep
'prone to' + something bad = likely to suffer it
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Lying face down' is the physical sense of 'prone', which does not take 'to accidents'. 'Protected from' is the opposite. 'Responsible for' would blame the teenagers for causing accidents, which the sentence does not say.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about starting school later in the morning?

options.text: It guarantees better examination results for every student.
It brings clear benefits but also some practical difficulties.
It has been rejected by most sleep experts as impractical.
It matters only for students who use their phones at night.

solution.concept: Inference: weighing benefits and costs stated in one paragraph
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 lists benefits (longer sleep, better attendance, less tiredness) and then says 'The change is not easy to make', listing bus routes, parents' hours and activities. Both sides are stated.
steps: Benefits: students sleep longer, attend more, arrive less tired
Costs: bus routes, parents' hours, activities
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts 'the effect on examination results varies'. C contradicts the experts' support in paragraph 5. D ignores the passage's main point that the cause is biological, not phone use.
solution.final_answer: Option B: It brings clear benefits but also some practical difficulties.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude towards sleepy teenagers?

options.text: critical, blaming them for wasting their nights on screens
indifferent, treating their sleep as a private family matter
alarmed, predicting a collapse in school standards
understanding, seeing their tiredness as partly biological

solution.concept: Tone: read the author's own conclusion
solution.explanation: The last paragraph says 'A sleepy teenager is not necessarily lazy; he or she may be fighting biology', and suggests schools take this into account. That is an understanding, sympathetic attitude.
steps: Key line: 'not necessarily lazy ... fighting biology'
The author defends rather than blames
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts the author, who says screens 'play a part' but points to a deeper cause. B is wrong because the author discusses what schools should do. C exaggerates: no collapse of standards is predicted.
solution.final_answer: Option D: understanding, seeing their tiredness as partly biological

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why may a price of ₹499 seem much lower than ₹500 to a shopper?

options.text: Shoppers give the most weight to the first digit that they read.
Shoppers carefully work out the value of saving a single rupee.
Shops usually round such prices down further at the billing counter.
Odd prices are printed in smaller type on most shop price tags.

solution.concept: Locating a stated explanation
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: people 'read a price from left to right and give most weight to the first digit', so ₹499 is registered as 'four hundred and something'.
steps: Most weight on the first digit (4, not 5)
solution.why_others_wrong: B contradicts the passage, which calls the one-rupee saving 'trivial'. C and D are not mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Shoppers give the most weight to the first digit that they read.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, do sellers of luxury goods often avoid charm prices?

options.text: Luxury buyers always pay by card and dislike odd amounts.
Charm prices suggest bargains rather than quality and confidence.
The law requires costly items to be sold at round prices.
Luxury goods are too expensive for the first-digit effect to work.

solution.concept: Inference: 'For the same reason' links back to the message charm prices carry
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 says charm prices signal discounts and bargains, and 'For the same reason, sellers of luxury goods often avoid them'; a round price 'suggests quality and confidence rather than a hunt for bargains'.
steps: Charm price = signal of a bargain
Luxury sellers want to signal quality instead
So they avoid charm prices: option B
solution.why_others_wrong: A and C are never mentioned. D is plausible on its face but is not the reason given; the passage links the weakening of the first-digit effect to careful thinking, not to high prices as such.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Charm prices suggest bargains rather than quality and confidence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which situation does the passage say that the pull of the first digit weakens?

options.text: When the shop is offering a genuine discount on the item
When buyers are in a hurry and comparing many items
When buyers think carefully before a major purchase
When the price is quoted as a round figure

solution.concept: Locating a stated condition
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'When buyers think carefully, as they do before purchasing a house or a car, the pull of the first digit weakens.'
steps: Condition: careful thinking before a big purchase
solution.why_others_wrong: B is the opposite: paragraph 2 says the effect is strong when shoppers are in a hurry. A and D are not given as conditions that weaken the effect.
solution.final_answer: Option C: When buyers think carefully before a major purchase

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What change does the author connect with the spread of digital payments?

options.text: Shoppers paying by phone may stop noticing the first digit.
Card fees may push sellers towards round prices on all goods.
Odd prices may soon be barred for payments made through apps.
With no coins to handle, reactions to odd prices could shift.

solution.concept: Inference: reading a cautious claim exactly
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'as digital payments replace cash, the practical nuisance of receiving small change has disappeared, which may alter how shoppers respond to odd prices.'
steps: Effect: the nuisance of small change has gone
Possible result: responses to odd prices may change: option D
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are cautious-sounding guesses that the passage never makes: it links digital payments only to the disappearance of the small-change nuisance, not to the first digit, card fees or any ban.
solution.final_answer: Option D: With no coins to handle, reactions to odd prices could shift.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'persistence' as used in the passage ('the persistence of the ninety-nine suggests that sellers find it useful')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: persistence (of a practice) = its continuing to exist
solution.explanation: The charm price has been used 'for more than a century' and is still everywhere. Its persistence is its continued existence over a long time, which suggests sellers find it useful.
steps: Context: a pricing habit used for over a century
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Sudden return' and 'gradual decline' contradict a practice that has never gone away. 'Stubborn insistence' is the sense used of a person who keeps demanding something, not of a pricing habit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Prices carry messages that sway buyers beyond simple arithmetic.
Charm prices fool every shopper and ought to be banned by law.
Luxury sellers earn more than shops that rely on odd prices.
Digital payments have made the psychology of pricing irrelevant.

solution.concept: Main idea: the author's conclusion in the last paragraph
solution.explanation: The passage explains how charm prices work, what they signal and where the effect weakens, and concludes that 'a price is not just a number but a piece of communication' that buyers read more into than arithmetic justifies.
steps: Paras 1–3: how and why charm prices work
Para 5: a price is communication: option A
solution.why_others_wrong: B overstates ('every shopper') and invents a call for a ban. C is never compared. D contradicts the passage, which says digital payments 'may alter' responses, not that pricing psychology no longer matters.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Prices carry messages that sway buyers beyond simple arithmetic.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, was lantana first brought to India?

options.text: To feed cattle during the dry months
To provide stems for weaving furniture
To decorate gardens with its bright flowers
To shield railway lines from forest fires

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1: the shrub 'was brought to India as an ornamental plant for gardens', and 'Its small, bright flowers made it popular'.
steps: Purpose: an ornamental plant for gardens
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts the passage: the leaves are toxic to livestock. B describes a much later use found by a few communities. D twists the later hedge planting along railway lines; the passage links the stems to feeding fires, not preventing them.
solution.final_answer: Option C: To decorate gardens with its bright flowers

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT given in the passage as a reason why lantana spreads so easily?

options.text: Birds eat its berries and scatter the seeds widely.
It grows quickly in open and disturbed ground.
Most animals avoid eating its toxic leaves.
Its roots release chemicals that kill nearby plants.

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 gives three reasons: birds scatter the seeds, it grows fast in disturbed ground, and animals avoid its toxic leaves so nothing keeps it in check. Chemicals from the roots are never mentioned.
steps: Fast growth in disturbed ground: stated (B)
Root chemicals: not in the passage: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are all stated in paragraph 2, so none of them can be the answer. D may sound scientific, but the question asks what the passage gives, and it does not mention root chemicals.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Its roots release chemicals that kill nearby plants.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, may predators leave areas where lantana dominates?

options.text: Their prey, such as deer, find less to eat there and move away.
The toxic leaves poison the predators that pass through the thickets.
Villagers clearing the thickets drive the predators out of the area.
Fires that start in lantana patches destroy the predators' dens.

solution.concept: Inference: following a chain of cause and effect
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: deer 'find less to eat where lantana dominates, and the predators that depend on them may follow them elsewhere'. The predators move because their prey moves.
steps: Predators that depend on deer follow: option A
solution.why_others_wrong: B wrongly applies the toxicity to predators; the passage says the leaves are toxic to livestock that might eat them. C and D are not given as reasons for predators leaving.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Their prey, such as deer, find less to eat there and move away.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the passage suggest about cutting lantana back without digging out its roots?

options.text: It is the quickest way to get rid of the plant for good.
It often lets the problem return, sometimes more strongly.
It is the method most forest departments now recommend.
It allows native grasses to spread back on their own.

solution.concept: Inference: reading the meaning of 'vigorous regrowth'
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'Cutting it back without digging out the roots often leads to vigorous regrowth.' Vigorous regrowth means the plant comes back strongly, so the problem returns.
steps: Find 'without digging out the roots' in paragraph 4
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts the regrowth. C is wrong: departments have adopted uprooting at the base instead. D contradicts the statement that cleared ground is quickly reinvaded unless native grasses are planted.
solution.final_answer: Option B: It often lets the problem return, sometimes more strongly.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'smothers' as used in the passage ('The consequences reach well beyond the plants it smothers')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: smother = cover something so completely that it cannot live or grow
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says lantana forms dense thickets that 'shade out the grasses and young trees beneath'. The plants it smothers are the ones it covers and kills in this way.
steps: Link back: thickets that shade out grasses and young trees
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Shelters' turns covering into protection, the opposite of the effect described. 'Feeds upon' wrongly makes lantana a parasite. 'Replaces gradually' misses the idea of covering and stifling.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: How does the author view the communities that make furniture and baskets from lantana?

options.text: Their work will soon remove lantana from Indian forests altogether.
Their work wastes effort that should go into proper removal.
Their work is a useful but limited response to a large problem.
Their work harms the forest by encouraging people to plant lantana.

solution.concept: Author's view: a balanced 'cannot ... but ...' judgement
solution.explanation: The last paragraph says 'Such efforts cannot remove lantana on their own, given the scale of the problem, but they turn a burden into a modest resource and give local people a reason to keep up the fight.'
steps: Limitation: cannot remove lantana on their own
Value: a modest resource and a reason to keep fighting
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts 'cannot remove lantana on their own'. B and D are criticisms the author never makes; the author presents the work positively.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Their work is a useful but limited response to a large problem.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, which of the following people is most likely to be caught in the sunk-cost trap?

options.text: An outside reviewer asked to assess a project for the first time
A manager deciding whether to continue a project he once proposed
An investor who agreed in advance on when to abandon a venture
A buyer who has not yet paid anything for the item in question

solution.concept: Inference: applying the condition under which the tendency grows stronger
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: the tendency 'tends to grow stronger when the person who made the original decision is also the one deciding whether to continue'. The manager who proposed the project fits exactly.
steps: Condition: the original decision-maker also decides whether to continue
solution.why_others_wrong: A and C describe the two safeguards in paragraph 5 (separate reviewers, conditions set in advance), which reduce the trap. D has no sunk cost at all, since nothing has been spent.
solution.final_answer: Option B: A manager deciding whether to continue a project he once proposed

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What is the author's view of the phrase 'protecting the investment' as officials use it?

options.text: It accurately describes the real purpose of most extra spending.
It is the technical term that economists use for sunk costs.
It subtly moves attention from future returns to past spending.
It is used only by private companies and never by governments.

solution.concept: Inference: the author's comment on a quoted phrase
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls it 'a phrase that quietly shifts attention from future returns to past costs'. The author sees it as a subtle distortion, not an accurate description.
steps: Author's comment: it 'quietly shifts attention' to past costs
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts the author's critical comment. B confuses it with 'sunk cost', the economists' term in paragraph 1. D is unsupported; officials of 'large organisations' generally are meant, and governments are named in paragraph 2.
solution.final_answer: Option C: It subtly moves attention from future returns to past spending.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following would the author regard as a justified reason for continuing a project?

options.text: Going on because so much has already been spent on it
Going on so that the planner escapes blame for the plan
Going on because stopping would admit the plan was wrong
Going on because finishing now costs less than starting anew

solution.concept: Inference: distinguishing what past spending produced from the spending itself
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4: continuing is justified 'not by the past spending itself but by what it has produced', for example a nearly finished building 'that makes completing the project cheaper than starting something new'.
steps: Justified: what the spending produced lowers the cost of finishing
Not justified: the spending itself, blame, pride
solution.why_others_wrong: A is the sunk-cost reasoning the passage rejects. B and C are the motives of avoiding blame and not admitting a mistake, which paragraphs 2 and 3 describe as the cause of the trap.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Going on because finishing now costs less than starting anew

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author mean by saying that the past should not 'hold it hostage' (the judgement of the future)?

options.text: The past should not keep our judgement captive and dictate its choices.
The past should not shield our judgement from outside dangers.
The past should not make our judgement of the future more predictable.
The past should not delay our judgement until a price has been paid.

solution.concept: Figurative language: to hold something hostage = to keep it captive and control what it can do
solution.explanation: A hostage is held captive and forced to act on the captor's terms. The author means past spending should inform decisions but must not control them, which is the sunk-cost trap the passage describes.
steps: Literal: a captor controls a hostage
Figurative: past costs controlling future decisions
solution.why_others_wrong: B reverses the image: a hostage-taker does not protect. C has no link with the image. D takes the ransom idea literally and misses the point about control.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The past should not keep our judgement captive and dictate its choices.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, may a rival with a better design fail to win customers from a dominant network?

options.text: Customers who switch lose access to everyone who stays on the larger network.
Better-designed services usually cost far more than the market leader's.
Regulators often bar new firms from entering markets that have tipped.
Users rarely notice any difference in design between rival services.

solution.concept: Inference: the cost of switching in a network market
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: a better-designed rival 'may struggle to break in, because a customer who switches gives up access to everyone who stays behind'. The value of the network, not the design, keeps customers in place.
steps: Find 'A rival with a better design' in paragraph 2
Reason: switching means losing everyone who stays
solution.why_others_wrong: B and D are never stated. C contradicts the passage, where regulators try to make switching easier, not to keep rivals out.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Customers who switch lose access to everyone who stays on the larger network.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the closest example of a 'network effect' as the passage defines it?

options.text: A bakery's bread improves after it installs a modern oven.
A shop lowers its prices because it buys its flour in bulk.
A video-calling app grows more useful as more relatives join it.
A car becomes cheaper to run when the price of fuel falls.

solution.concept: Applying a defined term to a new case
solution.explanation: A network effect exists when 'a product or service becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it'. A video-calling app is worth more to each user as more of the people he wants to call join it.
steps: Definition: value to each user rises with the number of users
Only the video-calling app fits: option C
solution.why_others_wrong: A is an improvement in the product itself. B is a cost saving from buying in bulk (economies of scale), which lowers the price but does not make the product more valuable as more people use it. D is a change in running costs. None depends on the number of other users.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A video-calling app grows more useful as more relatives join it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude towards dominant networks?

options.text: admiring, since dominance proves that the best product has won
hostile, since large networks bring users no real benefit
indifferent, since users can always move to a rival
balanced, valuing their convenience but wary of their power

solution.concept: Tone: weighing the author's praise and criticism
solution.explanation: The author calls the outcome for users 'mixed': a dominant network is 'convenient', and its benefits 'are real', but a firm whose customers cannot leave may raise fees, change rules or neglect privacy.
steps: Concern: power over customers who cannot leave
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts 'not necessarily because those firms offer the best product'. B contradicts 'which are real'. C contradicts the point that customers 'cannot easily leave'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: balanced, valuing their convenience but wary of their power

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, how does letting users carry their data to a competitor help them?

options.text: It makes the dominant network's own services more secure.
It lowers the cost to users of switching to a rival service.
It allows regulators to fix the fees charged to sellers.
It ensures that the network belongs to no single company.

solution.concept: Locating a stated effect
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4: letting users carry their data, such as contacts or ratings, to a competitor 'lowers the cost of switching'.
steps: Stated effect: lowers the cost of switching
solution.why_others_wrong: A reverses the passage, which warns that careless interoperability may weaken security. C is not mentioned. D describes the third remedy, a shared platform, not data portability.
solution.final_answer: Option B: It lowers the cost to users of switching to a rival service.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: verb + 'on' that means rely on
solution.explanation: Without modern equipment, the lights were the sailor's only guide, so he depended on them to know his position. 'Depend on' means rely on.
steps: The sailor needed the lights to know where he was
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Insisted on' means demanded firmly. 'Commented on' means remarked about. 'Operated on' is used of surgery. None means relied on.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the purpose of cleaning the glass
solution.explanation: Dirty glass makes a beam weaker. Keepers cleaned it so that the beam would not be dimmed (made less bright).
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Brightened' would make the sentence say they cleaned the glass so that the beam would not become brighter, which is illogical. 'Measured' and 'painted' do not describe what dirt does to a beam.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the next sentence explains the blank
solution.explanation: The next sentence says lamps 'switch on by themselves' and faults are reported to a distant control room. The lighthouses now run by machine: they have been automated.
steps: Next sentence: lamps switch on by themselves
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Abandoned' and 'demolished' contradict the lamps that still switch on every evening. 'Repainted' has nothing to do with lamps working on their own.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: what satellite navigation changed
solution.explanation: Ships can now find their position by satellite, so they need the lights less. The lights have become less essential (necessary) than they once were.
steps: Effect: ships rely less on the lights
solution.why_others_wrong: Satellite navigation does not make the lights less 'visible' or less 'colourful'. 'Less expensive' has no link with satellite navigation and does not explain why the keeper's job disappeared.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'that draws tourists'
solution.explanation: The paragraph describes towers opened to visitors, with views and museums. Something a town proudly displays and that draws tourists and their money is a showpiece.
steps: Paragraph: towers opened to visitors, museums
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Burden' and 'barrier' are the opposite of something that brings visitors and money. A 'warning' does not draw tourists; it keeps people away.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (6). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: fixed expression 'tell (someone) the truth'
solution.explanation: Electronic systems can fail. Seeing a familiar beam lets the captain check at once whether his instruments are correct, that is, whether they are telling him the truth.
steps: The beam lets him check whether they are right
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Telling him the time', 'the story' and 'the news' do not express whether the instruments are correct.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'yet it continues' signals that the practice is forbidden
solution.explanation: 'Yet it continues' shows a contrast: the practice goes on in spite of the law. So the law forbids it: it is prohibited. The last paragraph's mention of 'a ban' confirms this.
steps: The law must be against the practice
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Encouraged', 'permitted' and 'rewarded' remove the contrast with 'yet it continues' and clash with the 'ban' in the last paragraph.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'turns the problem into ...' needs something useful
solution.explanation: The paragraph shows straw being used to grow a saleable crop and then as manure. The problem becomes something useful: a resource.
steps: 'turns the problem into' → the opposite of a problem
Following sentences: straw grows mushrooms and manure
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Burden', 'hazard' and 'dispute' are themselves problems, so turning a problem into one of them makes no sense with the useful outcomes that follow.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: verb + 'to the fields as manure'
solution.explanation: The leftover material goes back to the fields where the straw came from, 'improving the soil that produced the straw in the first place'. It is returned to the fields.
steps: Pattern: be ___ to the fields as manure
Clue: the soil that produced the straw
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Restricted to' and 'confined to' mean limited to, which does not describe using the material as manure. 'Exported to the fields' is not idiomatic; export means send to another country.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the cooperatives answer the two difficulties just named
solution.explanation: The two difficulties are quick access to buyers and a lack of the knowledge needed to keep beds free of disease. Cooperatives 'collect the produce' (buyers) and provide training (knowledge).
steps: Difficulty 1: access to buyers → cooperatives collect the produce
Difficulty 2: lack of knowledge → cooperatives provide training
solution.why_others_wrong: Tractors, fertiliser and land are not among the difficulties described; the passage says a small shed and some sheeting are enough.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'one of several ___, along with machines ... and plants ...'
solution.explanation: Mushroom growing, straw-mixing machines and fuel plants are all ways of dealing with the straw instead of burning it. They are solutions.
steps: Items grouped together: mushrooms, machines, fuel plants
solution.why_others_wrong: They are not 'problems' or 'causes' of burning; the next sentence says they can reduce it. 'Crops' does not describe machines or fuel plants.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (6). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: paired adjectives with 'practical and ___'
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 says burning continues 'because the alternatives seem costly or slow'. Farmers will adopt the alternatives only if they are practical and affordable, answering the 'slow' and 'costly' objections.
steps: Para 1: alternatives seem costly or slow
Measures work only if they meet these objections
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fashionable' is irrelevant to farmers' choices. 'Compulsory' clashes with 'if farmers find them'. 'Complicated' would be a reason not to adopt them.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (1) may be wrongly used: 'To some observers this seems reasonable: gold pays no interest, costs money to store and guard'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the colon introduces reasons why the practice looks strange
solution.explanation: After the colon, the passage lists gold's drawbacks (no interest, storage costs, price swings) and then asks why a central bank should keep so much of it. These reasons make the practice seem strange, not reasonable. 'Curious' (odd, puzzling) fits.
steps: After the colon: drawbacks of holding gold
Followed by the puzzled question 'Why should ...?'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Prudent' and 'natural' would, like 'reasonable', present the practice as sensible, which contradicts the list of drawbacks and the question. 'Reasonable' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (2) may be wrongly used: 'gold is not anyone's promise to pay, so it cannot be defaulted on'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: 'default on' = fail to repay a debt
solution.explanation: A bond is a promise to pay, and the borrower can default on it (fail to pay). Gold is no one's promise, so no one can default on it. 'Defaulted' is correct.
steps: Contrast: bond (a promise to pay) vs gold (no promise)
A promise can be broken = defaulted on
'cannot be defaulted on' fits: no replacement
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Cannot be repaid on' and 'cannot be guaranteed on' are not idiomatic and lose the contrast with a broken promise. 'Cannot be traded on' is false and has nothing to do with the 'promise to pay'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (3) may be wrongly used: 'gold has tended to hold its value or even rise, which makes it a risky hedge against turmoil'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: 'which makes it ...' must follow from the good behaviour just described
solution.explanation: An asset that holds its value or rises when confidence falls is good protection in a crisis. That makes it a dependable hedge, not a 'risky' one.
steps: Gold holds or gains value in crises
Therefore it is a good hedge
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Costly' is a drawback (raised by the critics later), not something that follows from gold holding its value. 'Temporary' has no support in the sentence. 'Risky' contradicts the clause before it, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (4) may be wrongly used: 'Gold also helps central banks concentrate their reserves ... adding gold spreads the risk'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the next sentences describe spreading risk
solution.explanation: The paragraph explains that holding mainly one currency is risky and that 'adding gold spreads the risk'. Spreading reserves across different assets is diversifying them; 'concentrate' says the opposite.
steps: Problem: reserves mainly in one currency
Solution: adding gold spreads the risk
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Liquidate' (turn into cash, sell off) has nothing to do with spreading risk across assets. 'Value' their reserves does not match 'adding gold spreads the risk'. 'Concentrate' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (5) may be wrongly used: 'several central banks in emerging economies have been reducing their gold holdings steadily, partly for this reason and partly to lessen their dependence'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: 'for this reason' points back to the benefit of adding gold
solution.explanation: 'This reason' is that adding gold spreads risk, and lessening dependence on one country's financial system also calls for more gold, not less. Banks acting for these reasons would be increasing their holdings.
steps: 'for this reason' = adding gold spreads the risk
Lessening dependence on one country → hold more gold
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Auditing' and 'insuring' their holdings are not actions that spread risk or lessen dependence, and 'steadily' fits a change in size, not an audit. 'Reducing' contradicts both reasons given, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (6) may be wrongly used: 'holding a great deal of it amounts to costly insurance whose benefits are hard to measure'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the critics' objection decides the word
solution.explanation: The critics argue that money in gold earns no interest and could earn interest in bonds. Their point, introduced by 'but' after the concession 'may be prudent', is that holding a great deal of gold amounts to costly insurance. 'Costly' is correct.
steps: Critics: gold earns nothing; bonds earn interest
'but holding a great deal' = an objection
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Cheap' and 'reliable' would turn the critics' objection into praise. 'Compulsory' is false: no one forces central banks to hold gold.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The bank has launched (A) / a three-years savings plan (B) / for school students. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: A number + noun used as a compound adjective before another noun stays singular
solution.explanation: When a number and a noun together describe another noun, the noun is singular and the two are hyphenated: 'a three-year savings plan', just as we say 'a ten-rupee note' and 'a five-day week'.
steps: 'a three-years' → 'a three-year': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A uses the present perfect correctly. Part C ('for school students') is correct. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: a three-years savings plan

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The branch who opened (A) / near the bus stand last month (B) / is already crowded. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: near the bus stand last month

solution.concept: Relative pronouns: 'who' for people, 'which' or 'that' for things
solution.explanation: A branch is a place, not a person, so the relative pronoun must be 'which' or 'that': 'The branch which (or that) opened near the bus stand last month is already crowded.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct place-and-time phrase. Part C has a singular verb agreeing with 'branch'. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The branch who opened

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
On pension day, (A) / the waiting hall is not (B) / enough large for all the customers. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: enough large for all the customers.

solution.concept: 'Enough' comes after an adjective or adverb but before a noun
solution.explanation: With an adjective, 'enough' follows it: 'large enough', 'big enough'. ('Enough' comes before a noun: 'enough chairs'.) Correct: 'the waiting hall is not large enough for all the customers'.
steps: 'enough large' → 'large enough': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct time phrase. Part B ('the waiting hall is not') is correct. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: enough large for all the customers.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Hardly anyone (A) / turned up at the meeting (B) / because of the heavy rain. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Hardly anyone' (= almost nobody) is correct; no extra negative is needed
solution.explanation: 'Hardly anyone turned up' means almost nobody came. 'Hardly' is already negative, and the sentence correctly uses a positive verb with it. 'Turn up' (arrive) and 'because of' + noun are also correct.
steps: Part B: 'turned up at' = arrived at, simple past
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are each correct as shown in the steps. Changing A to 'Hardly no one' would create a double negative.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Of the two plans (A) / presented to the board, (B) / the second was clearly the best. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: the second was clearly the best.

solution.concept: When exactly two things are compared, the comparative ('better') is used, not the superlative ('best')
solution.explanation: The superlative is for three or more. With 'Of the two plans', the correct form is 'the second was clearly the better'.
steps: 'Of the two plans' → exactly two items
'the best' → 'the better': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Parts A and B correctly introduce the two plans. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: the second was clearly the best.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
These kind of errors (A) / are common among (B) / new clerks in their first month. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: new clerks in their first month.

solution.concept: 'Kind', 'sort' and 'type' agree with the demonstrative: 'this kind of', 'these kinds of'
solution.explanation: 'Kind' is singular, so it takes 'this': 'This kind of error is common ...'. For the plural, both words change: 'These kinds of errors are common ...'. 'These kind of' mixes a plural demonstrative with a singular noun.
steps: They must agree: 'these kinds of errors'
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B's plural verb 'are' agrees with the intended plural subject. Part C is a correct phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: These kind of errors

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The awareness camp was a failure, (A) / as a few villagers (B) / turned up to listen. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The awareness camp was a failure,

solution.concept: 'A few' (= some, a small but useful number) vs 'few' (= hardly any, not enough)
solution.explanation: The camp failed because almost nobody came. That negative idea needs 'few' (or 'very few'): 'as few villagers turned up to listen'. 'A few villagers' sounds positive and does not explain a failure.
steps: Result: the camp was a failure
Cause must be negative: hardly any villagers came
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is correct. Part C ('turned up to listen') is correct. B has an error of meaning, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: as a few villagers

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
On his doctor's advice, (A) / he stopped to eat sweets (B) / after his fiftieth birthday. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Stop + -ing' (give up an activity) vs 'stop + to-infinitive' (pause in order to do something)
solution.explanation: The doctor advised him to give up sweets, so he stopped eating them. 'He stopped to eat sweets' means he paused something else in order to eat sweets, the opposite of the advice.
steps: Context: doctor's advice → give up sweets
'stopped to eat' → 'stopped eating': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct phrase. Part C ('after his fiftieth birthday') is correct. B is grammatical on its own but wrong in meaning, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: he stopped to eat sweets

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The regional office has not yet decided (A) / if or not the branch (B) / will open on the second Saturday. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The regional office has not yet decided
will open on the second Saturday.

solution.concept: 'Whether or not' (or 'whether ... or not'); 'if' cannot be followed directly by 'or not'
solution.explanation: 'If' and 'whether' can both introduce an indirect question ('has not decided if the branch will open'), but only 'whether' can be followed immediately by 'or not': 'has not yet decided whether or not the branch will open on the second Saturday'.
steps: 'or not' placed straight after the conjunction
Only 'whether or not' is possible: 'if or not' → 'whether or not': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A correctly uses the present perfect with 'not yet'. Part C correctly uses 'will' inside the indirect question. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: if or not the branch

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The night guard (A) / noticed an asleep man (B) / lying on the bench outside the ATM. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: lying on the bench outside the ATM.

solution.concept: Some adjectives beginning with 'a-' (asleep, alive, afraid, alone) are used only after a verb, not before a noun
solution.explanation: We can say 'the man was asleep' but not 'an asleep man'. Before the noun we need 'a sleeping man': 'The night guard noticed a sleeping man lying on the bench outside the ATM.'
steps: 'an asleep man' → 'a sleeping man': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject. Part C ('lying on the bench ...') is a correct participle phrase. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: noticed an asleep man

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Not a single complaint (A) / has been received (B) / since the new system was introduced. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: since the new system was introduced.

solution.concept: 'Not a single' + singular noun takes a singular verb; present perfect with 'since' + a past point
solution.explanation: 'Not a single complaint' is singular, so 'has been received' is correct. The present perfect suits a period lasting up to now, and 'since' is followed by the simple past of the starting event ('was introduced').
steps: Part B: singular present perfect passive: correct
Part C: 'since' + simple past starting point: correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are each correct as shown in the steps. 'Have been received' would wrongly treat the subject as plural.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
In the strongroom, (A) / the three senior cashiers (B) / each has a separate locker. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: When 'each' comes after a plural subject, the verb agrees with the plural subject
solution.explanation: 'Each' at the start of a subject ('Each cashier has') takes a singular verb, but here the subject is 'the three senior cashiers' and 'each' follows it, so the verb is plural: 'the three senior cashiers each have a separate locker'.
steps: 'each' after the subject does not change its number
'each has' → 'each have': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct place phrase and part B a correct plural subject. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: each has a separate locker.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Being a public holiday, (A) / the branch remained closed (B) / and its ATM ran out of cash. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: and its ATM ran out of cash.

solution.concept: An introductory participle phrase must refer to the subject of the main clause; otherwise use an absolute phrase with its own subject ('It being ...')
solution.explanation: As written, 'Being a public holiday' describes 'the branch', as if the branch were a holiday. The day needs its own subject: 'It being a public holiday, the branch remained closed ...' (or 'As it was a public holiday, ...').
steps: Who or what was 'a public holiday'? The day, not the branch
Subject of the main clause: 'the branch'
Add a subject: 'It being a public holiday': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct main clause. Part C correctly joins a second clause. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Being a public holiday,

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**Why you did not inform** the bank as soon as your card was stolen?

solution.concept: Direct questions use question word order: question word + auxiliary + subject + base verb
solution.explanation: A direct question needs the auxiliary before the subject: 'Why did you not inform the bank ...?' (or 'Why didn't you inform ...?'). Statement order ('you did not') is used only in indirect questions.
steps: The sentence ends with '?' → direct question
Order: Why + did + you + not + base verb
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Why you had not informed' keeps statement order and changes the tense. 'Why did you not informed' uses a past form after 'did'. The original keeps statement order, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Why did you not inform

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**Instead of to wait** in the long queue, she paid the bill on the bank's app.

solution.concept: A preposition ('of' in 'instead of') is followed by a gerund (-ing form)
solution.explanation: 'Instead of' ends in the preposition 'of', and a verb after a preposition takes the -ing form: 'Instead of waiting in the long queue, she paid the bill on the app.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Instead to wait' drops the needed 'of'. 'Instead of wait' uses the base form after a preposition. The original uses a to-infinitive after 'of', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The roads are full of puddles this morning; it **must rain** heavily last night.

solution.concept: Modal of deduction about the past: must have + past participle
solution.explanation: The puddles are evidence from which the speaker concludes something about last night. A confident conclusion about the past is 'must have + past participle': 'it must have rained heavily last night'.
steps: Conclusion about a past event: 'last night'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Must be raining' is a deduction about the present. 'Should rain' expresses expectation or advice about the future. 'Must rain' cannot refer to last night, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**Supposing if you lose** your debit card, what will you do first?

solution.concept: Redundancy: 'supposing' already means 'if', so the two are not used together
solution.explanation: 'Supposing' (like 'suppose' and 'if') introduces a condition by itself. Using it with 'if' doubles the conjunction. Correct: 'Supposing you lose your debit card, what will you do first?'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Supposing if you will lose' keeps the doubled conjunction and adds 'will' in the condition. 'Suppose if you lost' keeps 'if' and changes the tense. The original doubles the conjunction, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**As far as the home loan**, the bank will decide on your application next week.

options.text: As far as the home loan goes on
So far as the home loan
As far as the home loan is concerned

solution.concept: The fixed expression is 'as far as X is concerned' (or 'as far as X goes')
solution.explanation: 'As far as' introduces a clause and needs a verb: 'As far as the home loan is concerned, the bank will decide on your application next week.' Without 'is concerned' the phrase is incomplete.
steps: 'As far as' + subject needs a verb
'As far as the home loan is concerned'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Goes on' is not the fixed completion. 'So far as the home loan' is incomplete in the same way as the original. The original is incomplete, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: As far as the home loan is concerned

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
I **have gone** to the bank's head office in Mumbai twice, so I know the way.
